title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene on chromosome 10q24.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping. We now report evidence that Heparanse 2 (HPSE2) is the culprit gene for the syndrome.
checks.explanation: HPSE2 is identified as the UFS gene in the 10q24 region the authors mapped.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and an abnormal facial expression, in which patients grimace when attempting to smile (Wang et al., 1997; Daly et al., 2010). Patients present with urinary tract infection and voiding dysfunction from neurogenic bladder. The bladder fails to void completely even though there is no anatomic outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage. Reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract puts patients at risk of kidney damage and renal failure (Daly et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, 1 of which was consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. Urinary findings included hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, and urethral valves. The bladder was abnormal, with trabeculation and diverticula associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes. Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition.

Urologic work-up showed mild neuropathic bladder in all cases, and most patients had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: Derbent et al. (2009) reported what they described as the first published case of urofacial syndrome in Turkey. The patient was diagnosed at 16 years of age after having been followed with a diagnosis of recurrent urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux. The authors noted that patients appear to be crying when they smile and that some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease.

paragraphs.text: From genetic analysis of 3 families, Elejalde (1979) concluded that the condition was probably autosomal dominant with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance. In contrast, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) concluded that inheritance was autosomal recessive, based on occurrence in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and an equal sex ratio. Homozygous mutations in the HPSE2 gene in affected individuals (Daly et al., 2010) confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) ran a genome screen in 20 selected patients using a combination of homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling. Marker D10S677 showed linkage to and association with UFS, with a significant excess of homozygosity in patients compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)). All 31 patients were homozygous for 2 closely linked markers, D10S1726 and D10S198, located approximately 5 cM telomeric to D10S677. Only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinations placed the UFS gene within a 1-cM interval defined by D10S1433 and D10S603 on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2003) built a genomic sequence map covering the whole UFS interval, which earlier studies had placed in a region of about 360 kb on 10q23-q24. They narrowed the disease interval to a 220-kb region that contained the ACDP1 gene and part of the GOT1 gene. Their analyses indicated that the same 10q gene was responsible in all UFS patients from multiple ethnic groups.

paragraphs.text: Pang et al. (2010) identified loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all UFS patients originating from Colombia, the United States, and France. HPSE2 encodes a 592-amino acid protein with a domain homologous to the glycosyl hydrolase motif of heparanase (HPSE). The authors suggested that HPSE2 may be important for the synergic action of muscles involved in facial expression and urine voiding.

clinical_synopsis.feature: End-stage renal disease in some patients
Incomplete bladder emptying without anatomic obstruction
Inverted facial expression; grimacing or appearing to cry when attempting to smile

paragraphs.text: In a patient with urofacial syndrome-1, whole-genome SNP mapping defined a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24. Within this region, Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene within the 16-Mb autozygous region in a patient with urofacial syndrome-1.

agent.process_note: I read all 12 files in full. Eleven contain abstracts only, and Teebi et al. (1989) has a title only, so I left it uncited. There were no full texts, so I could not find specific HPSE2 nucleotide or protein changes, patient counts or ancestry for the 2010 gene reports. The 10-kb deletion of exons 8-9 is the only variant specific enough to list, and its zygosity in the index patient is implied by autozygosity but not stated. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the HPSE2 MIM number is left out.
